newsitem.title: GERMANY: Global truck makers under burden of slow markets.
newsitem.headline: Global truck makers under burden of slow markets.

text.p: Global commercial vehicle makers, faced with a difficult 1996 due to regional economic slowdowns, are struggling under the weight of poor sales among heavier trucks, industry leaders said Thursday.

The difficult world market has been brutal to many truck manufacturers, particularly in Europe, with several having to offer generous deals to maintain market share as overall sales volumes remain steady or shrink.

"It's going to get tougher, tougher and tougher. We have to reduce costs or people are not going to stay in business," Tommy Rengman, executive vice president at Volvo Trucks, said in an interview at the IAA international truck exhibition.
Volvo was evidence of the industry's troubles, saying on Thursday its truck sales during the first eight months of 1996 slumped 17 percent to 41,900 trucks from the same 1995 period.

Rengman blamed the poor sales on North and South America, where he said "the markets have declined dramatically". The Swedish group's sales were helped by a seven percent increase in European sales, notably from its smaller vehicles.
Volvo is following the lead of carmakers in seeking to cut costs through economies of scale and modular design, as shown in the new Volvo FLC 7.5 tonne truck unveiled at the show.
Rengman said Volvo is targeting to reduce the number of parts in its worldwide production system to 25,000 by the year 2000 from a level of 41,000 parts in 1995.
"This gives us long-term economies of scale," he said.

The leader of MAN AG's truck division, Rudolf Rupprecht, also said greater efforts were needed to improve production capacity in the industry because of the "problematic" German commercial market and tough competition in Europe.
"Only in this way will we be able to keep up a positive trend," he said. "The prerequisite for this is naturally an upturn in the market in the second half of our fiscal year."

France's Renault noted expectations for the heavy vehicle market in Europe to fall four percent in 1996 to 250,000 vehicles and said manufacturers have to confront the slow European economy "all in a climate of stiff competition".

The strain of tough sales among heavier trucks was most evident at Europe's top truck producer, Mercedes-Benz AG, when Mercedes chief executive Helmut Werner said the group "has a fight on our hands" in the market for heavier trucks.
Werner has set ambitious goals for the unit, saying he wants a profit from European commercial truck sales in 1998 and a billion marks to be cut in costs.
Analysts said that led to strife with some managers, including Bernd Gottschalk who resigned in August as head of the truck division after he disagreed with Werner over the unit's future.

"Our truck business is enjoying varied degrees of success in Europe and overseas," Werner told journalists on Thursday, noting the Mercedes share of registrations in European trucks over six tonnes fell two percent over year-ago levels.
But while the sale of heavier trucks, mainly those weighing more than six tonnes, are having troubles, the sale of smaller transport vans and delivery trucks have been relatively strong.

In the van sector, Werner said Mercedes was "enjoying particular success" both in terms of sales figures and incoming orders. Mercedes sold 76,500 units, increasing its van sales in the west European market by 26 percent.
Mercedes, set to unveil its Vito and Sprinter vans at the show, said it now has a European market share in the class of 14 percent, 2.2 percentage points higher than year-ago levels.

Volkswagen AG also showed the stronger sales among lighter trucks, saying that its commercial vehicles sales through August in western Europe rose 13 percent to 112,000 vehicles, raising its market share to 11.8 percent from 11.1 percent.
VW, Europe's largest carmaker, said the gains were due to the introduction of new models and that the increase outpaced overall European market growth of four percent.

Wiedmann said he expected sales at the VW commercial truck unit, now structured as a separate brand within the VW group along with Audi, VW passenger cars, SEAT and Skoda, to total 10.5 billion to 11 billion marks for 1996.
